interest: This cross-reference sheet captures a key moment in the burgeoning relationship between the Ethiopian Empire and the Japanese Empire in the mid-1930s, just prior to the outbreak of the Second Italo-Ethiopian War. Because landlocked Ethiopia relied on the railway terminus at Djibouti in French Somaliland for maritime access, the dispatch of an official Ethiopian delegation to greet the Japanese naval training cruisers Iwate and Asama demonstrates Ethiopia's proactive diplomatic outreach to non-European powers. For diplomatic and naval historians, it reflects both Japan's expanding maritime training voyages in the Indian Ocean / Red Sea corridors and the U.S. State Department's tracking of Japanese-Ethiopian contacts during an era of heightened geopolitical sensitivity in the Horn of Africa.
overview: This file consists of a single-page Department of State document file note (cross-reference sheet) dated June 21, 1934, filed under decimal classification 894.3384/1. It cross-references despatch No. 1384 from Addison E. Southard, the American diplomatic representative in Ethiopia, which was originally filed under decimal number 784.94/10. The underlying despatch reports on the goodwill visit of the Japanese naval training vessels Iwate (recorded in the note as 'IWATA') and Asama to the port of Djibouti in French Somaliland, highlighting that the Ethiopian government dispatched an official delegation to Djibouti to formally greet the visiting Japanese ships.

subfiles.summary: A Department of State document file note dated June 21, 1934, directing the reader to file 784.94/10 for despatch No. 1384 from Addison E. Southard in Ethiopia. The note summarizes Southard's report regarding the visit of the Imperial Japanese Navy training ships Iwate (spelled 'IWATA') and Asama to the port of Djibouti in French Somaliland. It specifically records that an official Ethiopian delegation was sent to greet the visiting Japanese vessels.
